Continual learning systems must acquire new tasks without destroying performance on old ones, and the embedding space is where that tension plays out structurally: as new data reshapes the encoder's representational geometry, previously learned concepts either survive intact, drift, or collapse into new clusters. The central question here is whether the way you select examples for your replay buffer — random sampling, uncertainty-based selection, coverage-maximizing strategies like coreset methods, or gradient-based influence approaches — systematically determines how badly the embedding space fragments, meaning whether old-task representations become non-linearly separable, internally dispersed, or overwritten entirely. The key concepts to hold together are: catastrophic forgetting (the well-documented performance collapse), representational drift (subtler geometric displacement that can precede measurable forgetting), and the distinction between rehearsal fidelity (does replayed data accurately reconstruct the old manifold?) versus rehearsal diversity (does it cover enough of the manifold to constrain the encoder?). What a beginner misses is that buffer curation isn't just a data efficiency problem — a small, well-curated buffer can actively destabilize the embedding space if it over-represents boundary examples or outliers, because the encoder generalizes from those examples in ways that distort the dense interior of the old-task manifold. The expert worry is therefore not "do we remember enough?" but "does the geometric signal sent by our buffer examples preserve the topology of the original embedding region, and does our training objective even have a mechanism to enforce that?"

Recoverable fragmentation is characterized by representations that have drifted but remain locally consistent — the intra-class geometry is preserved even if the absolute position in embedding space has shifted, meaning a small number of labeled examples can re-anchor a linear probe or adapter without retraining the encoder. Permanent collapse, by contrast, occurs when the encoder has lost the feature dimensions that made old-task classes separable in the first place — the information is gone, not merely displaced, and no amount of fine-tuning on old data recovers it because the gradient signal has nowhere to attach. The measurable boundary that experts actually use is centered kernel alignment (CKA) between the original and post-continual-learning representations: empirically, Nguyen et al. (2021) and subsequent work on transfer rigidity show that CKA scores above roughly 0.7 between old-task layer activations correlate with fine-tuning recoverability, while scores below ~0.4 indicate the representational structure has been sufficiently destroyed that probing accuracy never recovers to baseline. A more local signal is intra-class variance relative to inter-class distance in the old-task subspace — recoverable drift shows inflated intra-class spread (the cluster smeared but not merged), while collapse shows intra-class variance approaching inter-class distance, meaning clusters have interpenetrated. Systems like DER++ (Buzzega et al., 2020) partially guard against collapse by replaying logits rather than just labels, which preserves more of the original output geometry and buys higher CKA retention, but this only works if the buffer actually samples interior manifold points rather than boundaries. The expert concern is that most continual learning benchmarks measure end-task accuracy and would report identical numbers for a drifted-but-recoverable encoder and a collapsed one — the distinction only surfaces if you explicitly probe intermediate representations, which most standard evaluations skip entirely.

The paradox arises because k-center and coreset methods select examples that maximally span the embedding space — by design, they oversample the boundary and low-density regions of the old-task manifold while leaving the dense interior underrepresented in the buffer. When the encoder is then trained on new tasks, the gradient signal from replayed boundary examples is disproportionately large (boundary points are harder, higher loss, higher gradient norm), which means the optimization preferentially reshapes the regions of embedding space that the old-task manifold's interior occupies — precisely the region with no replay coverage to resist that pressure. Toneva et al.'s work on "forgetting events" and subsequent analysis in class-incremental benchmarks shows that the examples most likely to be selected by coverage-maximizing strategies are also the examples with the highest "forgetting rate" under standard SGD — they sit near decision boundaries that new-task gradients directly attack. Concretely, in Split-CIFAR-100 experiments comparing random replay to herding/coreset selection at buffer size 200 per task, coreset methods sometimes show 3–8% worse final accuracy than random sampling under aggressive learning rates, a result that appears counterintuitive until you examine where the collapse is occurring geometrically. Random sampling, by contrast, draws proportionally from the dense interior, sending the optimizer a signal that is statistically representative of the full old-task distribution — the gradient from replayed data acts more like a true distributional anchor rather than a boundary-enforcement signal. The training regime dependency matters crucially: at low learning rates or with strong regularization (EWC penalties, learning rate warmup), coreset methods do better because boundary signal is useful for maintaining separation; it's specifically under high learning rate or momentum-heavy optimizers like Adam with large step sizes that the boundary-biased buffer becomes a liability, as the optimizer overshoots and the unprotected interior collapses.

Empirical evidence consistently shows that collapse originates in the later layers — specifically the last 2–3 layers before the projection head — while early convolutional or attention layers remain surprisingly stable across tasks; Raghu et al.'s SVCCA analysis and follow-on CKA work by Kornblith et al. show that lower layers converge to similar representations regardless of task sequence, while upper layers are where task-specific geometry lives and therefore where new-task gradients do the most damage. This makes intuitive sense because early layers learn low-level features (edges, textures, local patterns) that are shared across tasks and receive reinforcing gradient signal from new data, while later layers encode the compositional, class-discriminative structure that is directly competed over during new-task learning. Freezing early layers and allowing later layers to update freely — the approach taken by systems like PackNet and progressive freezing variants — does protect against low-level feature drift but produces a characteristic failure mode: the frozen early layers become a representational bottleneck, unable to extract features relevant to new tasks that genuinely require different low-level processing, so the system compensates by overloading the unfrozen upper layers, which then fragment faster under the increased representational burden. The opposite strategy — freezing later layers and fine-tuning only early layers — almost never works in practice because it assumes the old-task discriminative geometry in upper layers can remain valid while the features feeding into it change, which produces silent collapse: accuracy metrics look stable for several tasks then fall off a cliff when early-layer drift finally propagates upward and invalidates the frozen upper-layer structure. Layer-wise replay (sending old-task examples only through specific layers to generate targeted gradient corrections) is more surgical but introduces its own failure mode documented in progressive neural network variants: if the layer receiving replay signal is upstream of a layer absorbing heavy new-task gradient, the corrective signal is immediately overwritten within the same parameter update, making replay effectively invisible unless learning rate scheduling explicitly separates the two gradient sources in time or magnitude. The expert-level insight is that the question of where to protect is inseparable from the question of when within the optimization step — freezing and layer-wise replay both implicitly assume gradient locality that SGD with momentum actively violates.

This low-rank structure exists because final layers are doing a relatively constrained job — projecting a rich intermediate representation onto a small number of class logits — which means the parameter directions that actually matter for task performance span a subspace whose dimension is bounded roughly by the number of classes times a small multiple, not by the full layer width. KFAC exploits this by approximating the Fisher block for a layer as a Kronecker product of two smaller matrices (input covariance and output gradient covariance), and in continual learning this has been applied in KFAC-EWC and FROMP (Pan et al., 2020), where FROMP uses a functional regularizer anchored at inducing points selected to span the old-task output subspace — on Split-CIFAR-100 this recovers roughly 8–12% accuracy over diagonal EWC by capturing exactly the cross-parameter correlations diagonal methods miss. The interpretable correspondence is striking: the dominant eigenvectors of the KFAC Fisher blocks in final layers align closely with task-discriminative directions in representation space — concretely, if you project activations onto the top-k eigenvectors of the final layer's input covariance factor, you recover something close to a task identity subspace, where different tasks occupy geometrically separated regions whose separation is precisely what continual learning must preserve. Earlier layers do not show this clean low-rank structure — their Fisher blocks are higher rank and less interpretable, reflecting the fact that early features are shared and their curvature structure is diffuse across many directions simultaneously, which is why KFAC approximations applied to early layers yield much smaller accuracy gains and why the computational investment is rarely justified there. The practical implication is that a hybrid strategy — full KFAC protection on final layers where geometry is tractably low-rank, diagonal EWC or simple replay on earlier layers where it is not — captures most of the geometric benefit at a fraction of the cost, and this is roughly what systems like FROMP and variational continual learning (VCL) with layer-wise priors implement, though rarely with explicit acknowledgment that the justification is rank structure rather than mere computational convenience.

Gradient routing around identified subspaces is exactly what Gradient Projection Memory (GPM) (Saha et al., 2021) implements: it maintains a basis for the subspace spanned by old-task gradients and projects new-task gradient updates into the null space of that basis, ensuring updates are orthogonal to directions that mattered for previous tasks — on Split-CIFAR-100 and Split-TinyImageNet this yields 5–15% better retention than EWC variants precisely because it operates on gradient geometry rather than parameter penalties. The orthogonality assumption is GPM's central vulnerability: the method works cleanly when tasks are dissimilar enough that their gradient subspaces are nearly orthogonal, but empirically on fine-grained benchmarks where tasks share visual structure (e.g., superordinate/subordinate category splits), the subspace overlap can consume 40–60% of available dimensions, leaving so little null space that new-task gradients are either heavily distorted or the projection is abandoned entirely. When subspaces are merely oblique rather than orthogonal, the system faces a geometric tradeoff with no clean solution: projecting fully into the null space of old tasks preserves old geometry but cripples new-task learning; allowing partial overlap means accepting controlled interference, but the interference is asymmetric — the older task's subspace, having been built on more training, tends to dominate and crowd out the newer task's discriminative directions, producing a recency-reversed forgetting pattern opposite to the usual catastrophic forgetting. OWM (Orthogonal Weights Modification) and TRGP (Trust Region Gradient Projection) (Lin et al., 2022) attempt to handle oblique cases by scaling the projection based on subspace similarity rather than applying a hard null-space constraint — TRGP specifically uses a trust-region around the old-task subspace to allow bounded interference, recovering 3–6% accuracy on benchmarks where GPM degrades, but this introduces a hyperparameter (the trust radius) that must be tuned per task-pair similarity, which is impractical without knowing task relationships in advance. The deeper structural problem is that oblique subspaces reveal a fundamental capacity limitation: if k tasks each require d discriminative dimensions and the total parameter space has dimension D, clean routing is only possible when k×d << D, and in realistic continual learning scenarios with many tasks this inequality eventually fails, at which point gradient routing methods all converge to the same failure mode — they are implicitly doing lossy compression of task geometry into insufficient space, and the compression artifacts appear as systematic confusion between tasks whose discriminative subspaces were forced to share dimensions. What no current gradient routing method handles well is the dynamic case where the same input region is discriminative for multiple tasks in conflicting ways — the subspace identified by KFAC or gradient accumulation reflects the average geometry over a task, but individual examples near subspace intersections experience interference that task-level routing statistics cannot detect or prevent.

Task ordering bias is empirically robust and mechanistically well-understood: earlier tasks claim gradient subspace dimensions first, and because projection methods like GPM build their null-space constraint incrementally, later tasks are forced into whatever dimensions remain — Saha et al.'s own GPM experiments show variance of 8–12% in final accuracy across different task orderings on Split-CIFAR-100, with tasks learned early consistently outperforming tasks learned late when subspace overlap is high. The mechanism is a first-mover advantage in parameter space: early tasks shape the curvature structure of the loss landscape before any projection constraints exist, effectively pre-conditioning the Fisher and second-moment estimates in ways that make the parameter space intrinsically more sensitive to early-task directions, so even methods that don't explicitly use subspace projection inherit this bias through their optimizer state. Critically, this bias does not diminish with scale — it compounds, and the compounding follows a predictable pattern documented in Veniat et al.'s modular continual learning analysis: each new task finds a progressively more constrained null space, so the effective learning rate for new tasks (measured as the norm of the unprojected gradient component) decays roughly as 1/√k for k tasks under uniform subspace growth assumptions, meaning the 10th task has access to roughly 30% of the gradient signal available to the first task even under ideal projection. The geometry of this compounding differs qualitatively between two regimes: when tasks are dissimilar, subspace growth is roughly additive and the decay is gradual; when tasks are similar (sharing discriminative features), subspaces overlap heavily and the null space collapses superlinearly, producing sudden failure after a threshold number of tasks rather than graceful degradation — this threshold behavior has been observed empirically at around 15–20 tasks on CIFAR-based benchmarks with standard encoder widths. Attempts to mitigate ordering bias through task-agnostic subspace averaging (maintaining a running mean of gradient subspaces rather than a union) reduce variance across orderings but introduce a new failure mode: the averaged subspace represents no single task's geometry accurately, so protection is diffuse and all tasks suffer moderate interference rather than early tasks winning cleanly. The most honest finding in the literature is that ordering bias is fundamentally a symptom of insufficient model capacity relative to the cumulative discriminative geometry required — Rusu et al.'s Progressive Neural Networks sidestep it entirely by allocating new capacity per task, but this trades ordering bias for linear parameter growth, suggesting that any fixed-capacity system operating near its geometric limits will exhibit ordering sensitivity as an irreducible property.
